Juvenile Litopenaeus stylirostris in culture reach a wet body mass of 34.9 grams [Wwp = 34.9 grams] at the onset of sexual maturation, a value derived from length-weight relationships based on the total length at puberty of 17 centimeters. This developmental milestone coincides with an abdominal length of 10.9 cm [Lp = 10.9 cm], a measurement that does not differ between the sexes, as both males and females attain the same abdominal length at puberty of 10.9 cm [Lp = 10.9 cm]. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) rose to approximately 14% [GSI = approximately 14%] under thermal conditions of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].

In adult females of the blue shrimp, the maximum recorded wet mass reaches 86.4 grams [Wwi = 86.4 grams], corresponding to the ultimate wet weight estimated from a total length of 23 centimeters. This asymptotic body size is situated in the upper range for penaeid shrimps. In contrast, the ultimate abdominal length for females is 16.15 centimeters [Li = 16.15 centimeters], while males achieve a somewhat smaller ultimate abdominal length of 15.25 centimeters [Li = 15.25 centimeters], indicating a subtle but consistent sexual dimorphism in body architecture. The disparity in abdominal length is thought to reflect the greater space required for ovarian development and egg brooding in females. These morphometric differences may also influence differential mortality rates between sexes, as larger bodies in females require more energy to sustain basal maintenance requirements over the lifetime.

Neonates emerge from the egg at a wet weight at birth of just 0.000274 grams [Wwb = 0.000274 grams], a remarkably small mass that is typical of planktonic crustacean larvae among caridean and penaeid shrimps. This value is comparable to the hatchling mass reported for Palaemonetes varians, indicating a conserved pattern of larval provisioning within the infraorder Caridea. The newly hatched nauplius larva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves during the early stages before it initiates first exogenous feeding. The trophic switch from yolk absorption to active filter feeding marks a critical transition in larval energetics. At this point, the exogenously feeding larva must locate suitable phytoplankton concentrations in the water column to sustain growth through successive zoeal stages, a process that is highly temperature-dependent.

Longevity records for Litopenaeus stylirostris indicate a lifespan of approximately 620 days [am = approximately 620 days] under stable conditions at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a relatively short duration for a marine decapod of its moderate size. This maximum lifespan is ecologically constrained by the warm, productive environments this species inhabits, where rapid growth is traded against elevated metabolic costs. The lifespan is comparable to estimates for other fast-growing tropical penaeids such as Fenneropenaeus indicus. Following the larval metamorphosis, the post-metamorphic juvenile can grow rapidly through successive moulting events, each representing an ecdysis event where the exoskeleton is shed to allow for an increase in size. This accelerated growth phase is essential for reaching reproductive maturity before the onset of age-related physiological deterioration.

Morphometric and life history data for this species reveal that the abdominal length at puberty is consistently 10.9 centimeters [Lp = 10.9 centimeters], a value that appears invariant between sexes and supports the view that both males and females invest similarly in reaching a threshold body size before initiating gametogenesis. At this point, females have a wet mass at puberty of approximately 34.9 grams [Wwp = approximately 34.9 grams], a body size that permits successful ovarian development and spawning. Comparing these size thresholds with the ultimate body dimensions, females can grow an additional 5.25 centimeters in abdominal length after puberty, reaching the ultimate abdominal length of 16.15 centimeters [Li = 16.15 centimeters], while males add about 4.35 centimeters to attain the ultimate abdominal length of 15.25 centimeters [Li = 15.25 centimeters]. The lifespan of roughly 620 days [am = roughly 620 days] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] thus offers a relatively narrow window for multiple spawning events, and females likely allocate a substantial fraction of their time to reproductive effort once the initial size threshold is crossed.
